title: An OpenAI Strategist Says AI Labs Should Rival Government Power
excerpt: For years, the argument over artificial intelligence has followed a familiar script. Technology companies build increasingly powerful systems, governments
content_html:
For years, the argument over artificial intelligence has followed a familiar script. Technology companies build increasingly powerful systems, governments struggle to keep up, and Silicon Valley warns that politicians risk regulating a technology they do not understand. The disagreement is usually presented as a question of speed: how much oversight can AI tolerate without slowing innovation, weakening American competitiveness or handing an advantage to China?

Dean Ball is raising a more fundamental question.

Ball, who recently joined OpenAI as Head of Strategic Futures, has argued that frontier AI labs could become a “counterbalance to government.” Before joining the company, he described the organizations building the most advanced AI systems as a “new kind of institution under the sun.” Taken separately, those phrases might sound like the kind of ambitious language that surrounds almost everything in artificial intelligence. Taken together, they point to a much more consequential idea: that companies such as OpenAI may eventually become powerful enough that it no longer makes sense to think of them simply as corporations operating within rules set by the state.

That possibility is worth taking seriously, not because OpenAI has formally declared itself a rival to government — it has not — but because the technology industry is beginning to talk openly about a future in which the old hierarchy between governments and companies may no longer be so clear.

If the people building frontier AI are right about where this technology is heading, the implications go well beyond chatbots and productivity software. Advanced models could become deeply involved in software development, scientific research, medicine, education, cybersecurity, finance, military analysis and the operation of companies themselves. Governments will use these systems too. Intelligence agencies will use them. Public administrations will use them. Critical infrastructure operators will use them. At some point, a government may find itself trying to regulate an AI provider whose technology it simultaneously depends on.

That is not a normal relationship between a company and a regulator.

When a Technology Company Starts Looking Like an Institution

We have seen hints of this before. Governments already rely heavily on privately controlled cloud infrastructure. Apple can decide which software reaches more than a billion devices. Cloudflare can determine whether parts of the internet remain accessible under attack. Google has enormous influence over what information people find. Microsoft and Amazon operate infrastructure used by governments, militaries and critical industries around the world. None of those companies is sovereign in the constitutional sense, but each controls something that modern states cannot easily reproduce.

Artificial intelligence could take that dependency much further because AI is not infrastructure for a single narrow purpose. It is increasingly being developed as infrastructure for cognitive work itself.

If one system can write software, identify cyber vulnerabilities, analyze intelligence, design molecules, interpret legislation, generate political messaging and run business processes, then control over that system is a particularly unusual form of power. The company operating it may be able to influence entire categories of economic activity simply by changing prices, access rules, safety policies or technical capabilities. Decisions that currently look like product management could begin to resemble public policy.

This is what makes Ball’s idea interesting. There is, in fact, a respectable argument for institutions capable of counterbalancing governments. Democratic societies are deliberately full of them. Courts restrain elected politicians. Independent media expose government misconduct. Universities challenge political orthodoxy. Companies can reject unlawful demands. Civil society organizations exist precisely because concentrated state power is dangerous.

It would therefore be a mistake to assume that governments should automatically control the most capable AI systems simply because they are governments. States have their own record of surveillance, censorship, political coercion and technological abuse. A government with exclusive control of extremely powerful AI could be considerably more frightening than an AI industry with multiple independent actors.

Ball’s position is also more nuanced than a simple demand for deregulation. He has argued that certain future AI capabilities may be so dangerous that they “cannot realistically be left in private hands.” Systems capable of enabling biological weapons, highly advanced cyber operations or other forms of catastrophic harm could eventually require much stronger state involvement. In other words, the argument is not necessarily that private companies should replace governments. It is that the boundary between private and state power may have to be redrawn.

But once AI companies begin thinking of themselves as institutions capable of balancing governments, an obvious problem appears: governments have counterweights too. Who provides the counterweight to the AI companies?

Power Without Elections

That question is harder than it sounds because corporations were never designed to carry this kind of institutional legitimacy. Governments, for all their failures, are built around mechanisms intended to constrain power. Elected officials can be removed. Government decisions can be challenged in court. Public institutions operate under administrative law, constitutional limits, disclosure requirements and political scrutiny. These protections are imperfect and vary enormously between countries, but the principle is clear: the more coercive power an institution possesses, the more society expects mechanisms that make that power accountable.

The chief executive of an AI company is accountable in a very different way. Users do not vote for the board. Model policies are not passed by parliament. Internal safety decisions are generally not subject to freedom-of-information laws. A company can reorganize its leadership, rewrite its terms of service, discontinue a product or alter access to a model without anything resembling democratic due process.

For ordinary software, this is mostly a commercial matter. If an email application changes its terms, customers can complain or leave. But imagine an AI system that has become embedded in hospitals, universities, government departments and thousands of companies. Imagine that millions of workers rely on it to perform their jobs. Imagine that government agencies depend on it for cybersecurity or analysis.

At that point, the provider starts to look less like a software vendor and more like critical infrastructure.

And societies treat critical infrastructure differently for a reason. Banks face capital requirements because their collapse can damage everyone around them. Utilities have continuity obligations because electricity cannot simply disappear when supplying it becomes inconvenient. Telecommunications companies operate under rules that reflect their importance to society. The more indispensable a service becomes, the less comfortable we are leaving every decision about it entirely to the discretion of its owner.

If frontier AI genuinely becomes as important as its developers expect, similar questions will eventually arrive at the doors of AI companies. Should providers of economically critical models have continuity requirements? Should customers have some form of appeal if access is terminated? Should governments be able to require interoperability or emergency access under narrowly defined circumstances? Should there be independent auditing of systems used inside critical infrastructure? What happens if a model provider decides to withdraw from a country on which hospitals, businesses and public agencies have become dependent?

None of these questions has an easy answer, and rushing to regulate hypothetical problems can create problems of its own. But they illustrate why describing AI companies as a counterweight to government has consequences. Institutional power rarely comes without institutional obligations.

If AI Replaces Work, Who Replaces the Tax Base?

Taxation is one of those obligations, although probably not the most important one.

If AI systems automate a substantial amount of human work, governments may eventually face a practical fiscal problem. Modern tax systems collect enormous amounts of revenue from employment. Workers pay income taxes. Employers contribute payroll taxes. Wages fund consumption, which generates additional tax revenue. If some of that work moves from salaried employees to machine intelligence, the economic output may remain — or even grow dramatically — while the way governments collect revenue changes.

This does not automatically justify a punitive tax on artificial intelligence. Taxing emerging technology simply to make automation less attractive would be a good way to protect inefficient incumbents and push innovation elsewhere. But if AI companies are serious when they predict systems capable of replacing meaningful amounts of cognitive labor, policymakers are justified in asking whether the tax system should eventually follow the activity.

One proposal is a so-called token tax: a very small levy on large-scale commercial AI inference. Tokens are attractive because AI providers already meter them for billing, meaning usage is observable in a way that the work of a vaguely defined “robot” is not. Yet tokens are also an imperfect tax base. Different models tokenize language differently, reasoning systems may use large numbers of internal tokens, self-hosted models complicate enforcement, and tomorrow’s AI architectures may not use tokens in anything resembling today’s form. Compute, energy use, corporate profits or some other measure could prove more sensible.

The precise mechanism matters less at this stage than the principle behind the discussion. If increasingly large amounts of economic activity move from human labor toward privately controlled machine intelligence, governments will eventually have to decide whether existing systems for funding public services still make sense.

And taxation is only one example of a broader issue. Governments do things besides collect money. They provide continuity, security, dispute resolution, emergency response, infrastructure and, at least in democracies, a mechanism through which the public can challenge the exercise of institutional power. If AI companies want to be regarded as something more consequential than ordinary businesses — institutions capable of balancing states — the conversation cannot stop at their freedom from government control. It also has to include the responsibilities that come with becoming indispensable.

OpenAI Is Already Living the Contradiction

There is a particularly interesting tension here because Ball’s views should not be mistaken for an official declaration of OpenAI policy. OpenAI itself has advocated a durable federal framework for frontier AI and has spent considerable effort working with governments on safety, infrastructure and national security. The company is not publicly arguing that the state should disappear from AI governance.

If anything, the coexistence of those positions tells us something important about where the industry is heading. AI companies may want government involvement in some areas while resisting it in others. Governments may attempt to regulate AI companies while simultaneously becoming dependent on their technology. Both sides may possess leverage the other cannot easily ignore.

The relationship could eventually resemble something closer to negotiation between powerful institutions than traditional regulation of an industry.

That prospect should make people on both sides of the political spectrum slightly uncomfortable.

Those suspicious of government power should consider how much authority they are willing to place in corporations that have no democratic mandate. Those who favor strong regulation should consider whether concentrating advanced AI capabilities inside the state creates dangers of its own. And technology companies should recognize that the argument works both ways: if they want society to accept that frontier labs deserve independence because they can serve as a check on government, society is entitled to ask what checks should exist on them.

The Real Question Is Not Who Wins

Perhaps this entire discussion will turn out to be premature. AI progress may slow. Models may become commoditized. Open-source systems may prevent any small group of companies from accumulating the kind of power now being imagined.

But the people building frontier AI clearly do not believe that is the most likely future. They are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on infrastructure, recruiting policymakers and national-security officials, and openly discussing systems that could transform large parts of the economy.

We should probably take their ambitions seriously enough to think through what follows from them. The most consequential question raised by the idea of AI labs as a counterweight to government is not whether OpenAI, Anthropic or Google should be allowed to become powerful. They probably will become more powerful if their technology continues to improve.

The real question is what happens when a private company becomes powerful enough that “it’s just a company” is no longer an adequate description of what it is.

sentences.zh: 这就是鲍尔的想法变得有趣的原因。

sentences.en: There is, in fact, a respectable argument for institutions capable of counterbalancing governments.
sentences.zh: 事实上，对于能够制衡政府的机构存在着令人尊敬的论点。

sentences.en: Democratic societies are deliberately full of them.
sentences.zh: 民主社会故意充满这样的人。

sentences.en: Courts restrain elected politicians.
sentences.zh: 法院限制民选政客。

sentences.en: Independent media expose government misconduct.
sentences.zh: 独立媒体揭露政府不当行为。

sentences.en: Universities challenge political orthodoxy.
sentences.zh: 大学挑战政治正统。

sentences.en: Companies can reject unlawful demands.
sentences.zh: 公司可以拒绝非法要求。

sentences.en: Civil society organizations exist precisely because concentrated state power is dangerous.
sentences.zh: 民间社会组织的存在正是因为集中的国家权力是危险的。

blocks.html_en: It would therefore be a mistake to assume that governments should automatically control the most capable AI systems simply because they are governments. States have their own record of surveillance, censorship, political coercion and technological abuse. A government with exclusive control of extremely powerful AI could be considerably more frightening than an AI industry with multiple independent actors.

sentences.en: It would therefore be a mistake to assume that governments should automatically control the most capable AI systems simply because they are governments.
sentences.zh: 因此，仅仅因为政府是政府就认为政府应该自动控制最有能力的人工智能系统是错误的。

sentences.en: States have their own record of surveillance, censorship, political coercion and technological abuse.
sentences.zh: 各国都有自己的监视、审查、政治胁迫和技术滥用记录。

sentences.en: A government with exclusive control of extremely powerful AI could be considerably more frightening than an AI industry with multiple independent actors.
sentences.zh: 一个对极其强大的人工智能拥有独家控制权的政府可能比拥有多个独立参与者的人工智能行业更可怕。

blocks.html_en: Ball’s position is also more nuanced than a simple demand for deregulation. He has argued that certain future AI capabilities may be so dangerous that they “cannot realistically be left in private hands.” Systems capable of enabling biological weapons, highly advanced cyber operations or other forms of catastrophic harm could eventually require much stronger state involvement. In other words, the argument is not necessarily that private companies should replace governments. It is that the boundary between private and state power may have to be redrawn.

sentences.en: Ball’s position is also more nuanced than a simple demand for deregulation.
sentences.zh: 鲍尔的立场也比简单地要求放松管制更加微妙。

sentences.en: He has argued that certain future AI capabilities may be so dangerous that they “cannot realistically be left in private hands.”
sentences.zh: 他认为，未来的某些人工智能功能可能非常危险，以至于“实际上不能将它们留在私人手中”。

sentences.en: Systems capable of enabling biological weapons, highly advanced cyber operations or other forms of catastrophic harm could eventually require much stronger state involvement.
sentences.zh: 能够实现生物武器、高度先进的网络行动或其他形式的灾难性伤害的系统最终可能需要更强有力的国家参与。

sentences.en: In other words, the argument is not necessarily that private companies should replace governments.
sentences.zh: 换句话说，争论并不一定是私营公司应该取代政府。

sentences.en: It is that the boundary between private and state power may have to be redrawn.
sentences.zh: 私人权力和国家权力之间的界限可能需要重新划定。

blocks.html_en: But once AI companies begin thinking of themselves as institutions capable of balancing governments, an obvious problem appears: governments have counterweights too. Who provides the counterweight to the AI companies?

sentences.en: But once AI companies begin thinking of themselves as institutions capable of balancing governments, an obvious problem appears: governments have counterweights too.
sentences.zh: 但一旦人工智能公司开始将自己视为能够制衡政府的机构，一个明显的问题就会出现：政府也有制衡力量。

sentences.en: Who provides the counterweight to the AI companies?
sentences.zh: 谁为人工智能公司提供制衡力量？

blocks.html_en: Power Without Elections

sentences.en: Power Without Elections
sentences.zh: 没有选举的权力

blocks.html_en: That question is harder than it sounds because corporations were never designed to carry this kind of institutional legitimacy. Governments, for all their failures, are built around mechanisms intended to constrain power. Elected officials can be removed. Government decisions can be challenged in court. Public institutions operate under administrative law, constitutional limits, disclosure requirements and political scrutiny. These protections are imperfect and vary enormously between countries, but the principle is clear: the more coercive power an institution possesses, the more society expects mechanisms that make that power accountable.

sentences.en: That question is harder than it sounds because corporations were never designed to carry this kind of institutional legitimacy.
sentences.zh: 这个问题比听起来更难，因为公司从来就不是为了具有这种制度合法性而设计的。

sentences.en: Governments, for all their failures, are built around mechanisms intended to constrain power.
sentences.zh: 尽管政府有种种失败，但它们都是围绕旨在限制权力的机制建立的。

sentences.en: Elected officials can be removed.
sentences.zh: 民选官员可以被罢免。

sentences.en: Government decisions can be challenged in court.
sentences.zh: 政府的决定可以在法庭上受到质疑。

sentences.en: Public institutions operate under administrative law, constitutional limits, disclosure requirements and political scrutiny.
sentences.zh: 公共机构根据行政法、宪法限制、披露要求和政治审查运作。

sentences.en: These protections are imperfect and vary enormously between countries, but the principle is clear: the more coercive power an institution possesses, the more society expects mechanisms that make that power accountable.
sentences.zh: 这些保护并不完善，而且各国之间差异很大，但原则很明确：一个机构拥有的强制权力越多，社会就越期望有机制对这种权力负责。

blocks.html_en: The chief executive of an AI company is accountable in a very different way. Users do not vote for the board. Model policies are not passed by parliament. Internal safety decisions are generally not subject to freedom-of-information laws. A company can reorganize its leadership, rewrite its terms of service, discontinue a product or alter access to a model without anything resembling democratic due process.

sentences.en: The chief executive of an AI company is accountable in a very different way.
sentences.zh: 人工智能公司的首席执行官以一种截然不同的方式承担责任。

sentences.en: Users do not vote for the board.
sentences.zh: 用户不投票给董事会。

sentences.en: Model policies are not passed by parliament.
sentences.zh: 示范政策未经议会通过。

sentences.en: Internal safety decisions are generally not subject to freedom-of-information laws.
sentences.zh: 内部安全决策通常不受信息自由法的约束。

sentences.en: A company can reorganize its leadership, rewrite its terms of service, discontinue a product or alter access to a model without anything resembling democratic due process.
sentences.zh: 公司可以重组其领导层，重写其服务条款，停止产品或改变对模型的访问，而无需任何类似于民主正当程序的东西。

blocks.html_en: For ordinary software, this is mostly a commercial matter. If an email application changes its terms, customers can complain or leave. But imagine an AI system that has become embedded in hospitals, universities, government departments and thousands of companies. Imagine that millions of workers rely on it to perform their jobs. Imagine that government agencies depend on it for cybersecurity or analysis.

sentences.en: For ordinary software, this is mostly a commercial matter.
sentences.zh: 对于普通软件来说，这主要是商业问题。

sentences.en: If an email application changes its terms, customers can complain or leave.
sentences.zh: 如果电子邮件应用程序更改其条款，客户可以投诉或离开。

sentences.en: But imagine an AI system that has become embedded in hospitals, universities, government departments and thousands of companies.
sentences.zh: 但想象一下，人工智能系统已经嵌入医院、大学、政府部门和数千家公司。

sentences.en: Imagine that millions of workers rely on it to perform their jobs.
sentences.zh: 想象一下，数百万工人依靠它来完成工作。

sentences.en: Imagine that government agencies depend on it for cybersecurity or analysis.
sentences.zh: 想象一下政府机构依赖它来进行网络安全或分析。

blocks.html_en: At that point, the provider starts to look less like a software vendor and more like critical infrastructure.

sentences.en: At that point, the provider starts to look less like a software vendor and more like critical infrastructure.
sentences.zh: 到那时，提供商开始看起来不再像软件供应商，而更像关键基础设施。

blocks.html_en: And societies treat critical infrastructure differently for a reason. Banks face capital requirements because their collapse can damage everyone around them. Utilities have continuity obligations because electricity cannot simply disappear when supplying it becomes inconvenient. Telecommunications companies operate under rules that reflect their importance to society. The more indispensable a service becomes, the less comfortable we are leaving every decision about it entirely to the discretion of its owner.

sentences.en: And societies treat critical infrastructure differently for a reason.
sentences.zh: 社会对待关键基础设施的方式有所不同，这是有原因的。

sentences.en: Banks face capital requirements because their collapse can damage everyone around them.
sentences.zh: 银行面临资本要求，因为它们的倒闭可能会损害周围的每个人。

sentences.en: Utilities have continuity obligations because electricity cannot simply disappear when supplying it becomes inconvenient.
sentences.zh: 公用事业公司有连续性义务，因为当供电变得不方便时，电力不能简单地消失。

sentences.en: Telecommunications companies operate under rules that reflect their importance to society.
sentences.zh: 电信公司的运营规则反映了其对社会的重要性。

sentences.en: The more indispensable a service becomes, the less comfortable we are leaving every decision about it entirely to the discretion of its owner.
sentences.zh: 一项服务变得越不可或缺，我们就越不愿意将有关它的每一个决定完全交给其所有者自行决定。

blocks.html_en: If frontier AI genuinely becomes as important as its developers expect, similar questions will eventually arrive at the doors of AI companies. Should providers of economically critical models have continuity requirements? Should customers have some form of appeal if access is terminated? Should governments be able to require interoperability or emergency access under narrowly defined circumstances? Should there be independent auditing of systems used inside critical infrastructure? What happens if a model provider decides to withdraw from a country on which hospitals, businesses and public agencies have become dependent?

sentences.en: If frontier AI genuinely becomes as important as its developers expect, similar questions will eventually arrive at the doors of AI companies.
sentences.zh: 如果前沿人工智能真的像开发者所期望的那样重要，那么类似的问题最终也会出现在人工智能公司的门口。

sentences.en: Should providers of economically critical models have continuity requirements?
sentences.zh: 经济关键模型的提供商是否应该有连续性要求？

sentences.en: Should customers have some form of appeal if access is terminated?
sentences.zh: 如果访问被终止，客户是否应该提出某种形式的上诉？

sentences.en: Should governments be able to require interoperability or emergency access under narrowly defined circumstances?
sentences.zh: 政府是否应该能够在狭义的情况下要求互操作性或紧急访问？

sentences.en: Should there be independent auditing of systems used inside critical infrastructure?
sentences.zh: 是否应该对关键基础设施内部使用的系统进行独立审核？

sentences.en: What happens if a model provider decides to withdraw from a country on which hospitals, businesses and public agencies have become dependent?
sentences.zh: 如果模范提供者决定退出一个医院、企业和公共机构已经依赖的国家，会发生什么？

blocks.html_en: None of these questions has an easy answer, and rushing to regulate hypothetical problems can create problems of its own. But they illustrate why describing AI companies as a counterweight to government has consequences. Institutional power rarely comes without institutional obligations.

sentences.en: None of these questions has an easy answer, and rushing to regulate hypothetical problems can create problems of its own.
sentences.zh: 这些问题都没有一个简单的答案，而急于监管假设的问题可能会产生自己的问题。

sentences.en: But they illustrate why describing AI companies as a counterweight to government has consequences.
sentences.zh: 但它们说明了为什么将人工智能公司描述为政府的制衡会产生后果。

sentences.en: Institutional power rarely comes without institutional obligations.
sentences.zh: 机构权力很少伴随着机构义务。

blocks.html_en: If AI Replaces Work, Who Replaces the Tax Base?

sentences.en: If AI Replaces Work, Who Replaces the Tax Base?
sentences.zh: 如果人工智能取代工作，谁取代税基？

blocks.html_en: Taxation is one of those obligations, although probably not the most important one.

sentences.en: Taxation is one of those obligations, although probably not the most important one.
sentences.zh: 税收是这些义务之一，尽管可能不是最重要的一项。

blocks.html_en: If AI systems automate a substantial amount of human work, governments may eventually face a practical fiscal problem. Modern tax systems collect enormous amounts of revenue from employment. Workers pay income taxes. Employers contribute payroll taxes. Wages fund consumption, which generates additional tax revenue. If some of that work moves from salaried employees to machine intelligence, the economic output may remain — or even grow dramatically — while the way governments collect revenue changes.

sentences.en: If AI systems automate a substantial amount of human work, governments may eventually face a practical fiscal problem.
sentences.zh: 如果人工智能系统使大量人类工作实现自动化，政府最终可能会面临实际的财政问题。

sentences.en: Modern tax systems collect enormous amounts of revenue from employment.
sentences.zh: 现代税收制度从就业中收取巨额收入。

sentences.en: Workers pay income taxes.
sentences.zh: 工人缴纳所得税。

sentences.en: Employers contribute payroll taxes.
sentences.zh: 雇主缴纳工资税。

sentences.en: Wages fund consumption, which generates additional tax revenue.
sentences.zh: 工资为消费提供资金，从而产生额外的税收收入。

sentences.en: If some of that work moves from salaried employees to machine intelligence, the economic output may remain — or even grow dramatically — while the way governments collect revenue changes.
sentences.zh: 如果其中一些工作从受薪员工转移到机器智能，经济产出可能会保持不变，甚至大幅增长，而政府征收收入的方式也会发生变化。

blocks.html_en: This does not automatically justify a punitive tax on artificial intelligence. Taxing emerging technology simply to make automation less attractive would be a good way to protect inefficient incumbents and push innovation elsewhere. But if AI companies are serious when they predict systems capable of replacing meaningful amounts of cognitive labor, policymakers are justified in asking whether the tax system should eventually follow the activity.

sentences.en: This does not automatically justify a punitive tax on artificial intelligence.
sentences.zh: 这并不能自动证明对人工智能征收惩罚性税是合理的。

sentences.en: Taxing emerging technology simply to make automation less attractive would be a good way to protect inefficient incumbents and push innovation elsewhere.
sentences.zh: 对新兴技术征税只是为了降低自动化的吸引力，这将是保护效率低下的现有企业并推动其他地方创新的好方法。

sentences.en: But if AI companies are serious when they predict systems capable of replacing meaningful amounts of cognitive labor, policymakers are justified in asking whether the tax system should eventually follow the activity.
sentences.zh: 但如果人工智能公司在预测系统能够取代大量认知劳动时是认真的，那么政策制定者就有理由询问税收制度最终是否应该跟随这一活动。

blocks.html_en: One proposal is a so-called token tax: a very small levy on large-scale commercial AI inference. Tokens are attractive because AI providers already meter them for billing, meaning usage is observable in a way that the work of a vaguely defined “robot” is not. Yet tokens are also an imperfect tax base. Different models tokenize language differently, reasoning systems may use large numbers of internal tokens, self-hosted models complicate enforcement, and tomorrow’s AI architectures may not use tokens in anything resembling today’s form. Compute, energy use, corporate profits or some other measure could prove more sensible.

sentences.en: One proposal is a so-called token tax: a very small levy on large-scale commercial AI inference.
sentences.zh: 其中一项提议是所谓的“象征税”：对大规模商业人工智能推理征收极少量的税。

sentences.en: Tokens are attractive because AI providers already meter them for billing, meaning usage is observable in a way that the work of a vaguely defined “robot” is not.
sentences.zh: 代币很有吸引力，因为人工智能提供商已经对它们进行计费，这意味着使用情况是可以观察到的，而模糊定义的“机器人”的工作则不然。

sentences.en: Yet tokens are also an imperfect tax base.
sentences.zh: 然而，代币也是一个不完善的税基。

sentences.en: Different models tokenize language differently, reasoning systems may use large numbers of internal tokens, self-hosted models complicate enforcement, and tomorrow’s AI architectures may not use tokens in anything resembling today’s form.
sentences.zh: 不同的模型以不同的方式对语言进行标记，推理系统可能会使用大量内部标记，自托管模型使执行变得复杂，而明天的人工智能架构可能不会以类似于今天的形式使用标记。

sentences.en: Compute, energy use, corporate profits or some other measure could prove more sensible.
sentences.zh: 计算、能源使用、企业利润或其他一些衡量标准可能被证明更为明智。

blocks.html_en: The precise mechanism matters less at this stage than the principle behind the discussion. If increasingly large amounts of economic activity move from human labor toward privately controlled machine intelligence, governments will eventually have to decide whether existing systems for funding public services still make sense.

sentences.en: The precise mechanism matters less at this stage than the principle behind the discussion.
sentences.zh: 在这个阶段，精确的机制并不重要，讨论背后的原则才是重要的。

sentences.en: If increasingly large amounts of economic activity move from human labor toward privately controlled machine intelligence, governments will eventually have to decide whether existing systems for funding public services still make sense.
sentences.zh: 如果越来越多的经济活动从人力转向私人控制的机器智能，政府最终将不得不决定现有的公共服务资助系统是否仍然有意义。

blocks.html_en: And taxation is only one example of a broader issue. Governments do things besides collect money. They provide continuity, security, dispute resolution, emergency response, infrastructure and, at least in democracies, a mechanism through which the public can challenge the exercise of institutional power. If AI companies want to be regarded as something more consequential than ordinary businesses — institutions capable of balancing states — the conversation cannot stop at their freedom from government control. It also has to include the responsibilities that come with becoming indispensable.

sentences.en: And taxation is only one example of a broader issue.
sentences.zh: 税收只是更广泛问题的一个例子。

sentences.en: Governments do things besides collect money.
sentences.zh: 政府除了收钱之外还做一些事情。

sentences.en: They provide continuity, security, dispute resolution, emergency response, infrastructure and, at least in democracies, a mechanism through which the public can challenge the exercise of institutional power.
sentences.zh: 它们提供连续性、安全性、争端解决、应急响应、基础设施，以及至少在民主国家中公众可以挑战机构权力行使的机制。

sentences.en: If AI companies want to be regarded as something more consequential than ordinary businesses — institutions capable of balancing states — the conversation cannot stop at their freedom from government control.
sentences.zh: 如果人工智能公司希望被视为比普通企业更重要的东西——能够平衡国家的机构——那么对话就不能停止于它们不受政府控制的自由。

sentences.en: It also has to include the responsibilities that come with becoming indispensable.
sentences.zh: 它还必须包括变得不可或缺的责任。

blocks.html_en: OpenAI Is Already Living the Contradiction

sentences.en: OpenAI Is Already Living the Contradiction
sentences.zh: OpenAI 已经陷入矛盾之中

blocks.html_en: There is a particularly interesting tension here because Ball’s views should not be mistaken for an official declaration of OpenAI policy. OpenAI itself has advocated a durable federal framework for frontier AI and has spent considerable effort working with governments on safety, infrastructure and national security. The company is not publicly arguing that the state should disappear from AI governance.

sentences.en: There is a particularly interesting tension here because Ball’s views should not be mistaken for an official declaration of OpenAI policy.
sentences.zh: 这里有一个特别有趣的紧张关系，因为鲍尔的观点不应被误认为是 OpenAI 政策的官方声明。

sentences.en: OpenAI itself has advocated a durable federal framework for frontier AI and has spent considerable effort working with governments on safety, infrastructure and national security.
sentences.zh: OpenAI 本身倡导为前沿人工智能建立持久的联邦框架，并在安全、基础设施和国家安全方面与政府合作投入了大量精力。

sentences.en: The company is not publicly arguing that the state should disappear from AI governance.
sentences.zh: 该公司并未公开主张国家应该从人工智能治理中消失。

blocks.html_en: If anything, the coexistence of those positions tells us something important about where the industry is heading. AI companies may want government involvement in some areas while resisting it in others. Governments may attempt to regulate AI companies while simultaneously becoming dependent on their technology. Both sides may possess leverage the other cannot easily ignore.

sentences.en: If anything, the coexistence of those positions tells us something important about where the industry is heading.
sentences.zh: 如果说有什么不同的话，那就是这些职位的共存告诉了我们有关该行业发展方向的一些重要信息。

sentences.en: AI companies may want government involvement in some areas while resisting it in others.
sentences.zh: 人工智能公司可能希望政府参与某些领域，而在其他领域则抵制政府参与。

sentences.en: Governments may attempt to regulate AI companies while simultaneously becoming dependent on their technology.
sentences.zh: 政府可能会试图监管人工智能公司，同时变得依赖它们的技术。

sentences.en: Both sides may possess leverage the other cannot easily ignore.
sentences.zh: 双方都可能拥有对方无法轻易忽视的影响力。

blocks.html_en: The relationship could eventually resemble something closer to negotiation between powerful institutions than traditional regulation of an industry.

sentences.en: The relationship could eventually resemble something closer to negotiation between powerful institutions than traditional regulation of an industry.
sentences.zh: 这种关系最终可能类似于强大机构之间的谈判，而不是传统的行业监管。

blocks.html_en: That prospect should make people on both sides of the political spectrum slightly uncomfortable.

sentences.en: That prospect should make people on both sides of the political spectrum slightly uncomfortable.
sentences.zh: 这种前景应该会让政治光谱双方的人都感到有些不安。

blocks.html_en: Those suspicious of government power should consider how much authority they are willing to place in corporations that have no democratic mandate. Those who favor strong regulation should consider whether concentrating advanced AI capabilities inside the state creates dangers of its own. And technology companies should recognize that the argument works both ways: if they want society to accept that frontier labs deserve independence because they can serve as a check on government, society is entitled to ask what checks should exist on them.

sentences.en: Those suspicious of government power should consider how much authority they are willing to place in corporations that have no democratic mandate.
sentences.zh: 那些对政府权力持怀疑态度的人应该考虑他们愿意赋予没有民主授权的公司多少权力。

sentences.en: Those who favor strong regulation should consider whether concentrating advanced AI capabilities inside the state creates dangers of its own.
sentences.zh: 那些支持强有力监管的人应该考虑将先进的人工智能能力集中在国家内部是否会带来危险。

sentences.en: And technology companies should recognize that the argument works both ways: if they want society to accept that frontier labs deserve independence because they can serve as a check on government, society is entitled to ask what checks should exist on them.
sentences.zh: 科技公司应该认识到，这种争论是双向的：如果他们希望社会接受前沿实验室应该独立，因为它们可以对政府进行检查，那么社会就有权询问应该对它们进行什么检查。

blocks.html_en: The Real Question Is Not Who Wins

sentences.en: The Real Question Is Not Who Wins
sentences.zh: 真正的问题不是谁赢了

blocks.html_en: Perhaps this entire discussion will turn out to be premature. AI progress may slow. Models may become commoditized. Open-source systems may prevent any small group of companies from accumulating the kind of power now being imagined.

sentences.en: Perhaps this entire discussion will turn out to be premature.
sentences.zh: 也许整个讨论都为时过早。

sentences.en: AI progress may slow.
sentences.zh: 人工智能的进展可能会放缓。

sentences.en: Models may become commoditized.
sentences.zh: 模型可能会商品化。

sentences.en: Open-source systems may prevent any small group of companies from accumulating the kind of power now being imagined.
sentences.zh: 开源系统可能会阻止任何小规模公司积累现在所想象的那种力量。

blocks.html_en: But the people building frontier AI clearly do not believe that is the most likely future. They are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on infrastructure, recruiting policymakers and national-security officials, and openly discussing systems that could transform large parts of the economy.

sentences.en: But the people building frontier AI clearly do not believe that is the most likely future.

content_html_zh:
多年来，关于人工智能的争论一直遵循着熟悉的剧本。 科技公司建立了越来越强大的系统，政府努力跟上，硅谷警告政客们可能会冒着监管他们不理解的技术的风险。 这种分歧通常表现为速度问题：在不减缓创新、削弱美国竞争力或将优势拱手让给中国的情况下，人工智能可以容忍多少监督？

鲍尔院长提出了一个更根本的问题。

鲍尔最近加入 OpenAI，担任战略未来主管，他认为前沿人工智能实验室可能成为“制衡政府”。 在加入公司之前，他将构建最先进人工智能系统的组织描述为“阳光下的新型机构”。 单独来看，这些短语听起来像是一种雄心勃勃的语言，几乎涵盖了人工智能的所有领域。 总而言之，他们指出了一个更重要的想法：像 OpenAI 这样的公司最终可能会变得足够强大，以至于将它们简单地视为在国家制定的规则下运营的公司不再有意义。

这种可能性值得认真对待，不是因为 OpenAI 已正式宣布自己是政府的竞争对手——事实上它还没有——而是因为科技行业开始公开谈论未来，政府和公司之间的旧等级制度可能不再那么清晰。

如果构建前沿人工智能的人们对这项技术的发展方向是正确的，那么其影响将远远超出聊天机器人和生产力软件的范畴。 先进的模型可以深入参与软件开发、科学研究、医学、教育、网络安全、金融、军事分析和公司本身的运营。 政府也将使用这些系统。 情报机构将使用它们。 公共管理部门将使用它们。 关键基础设施运营商将使用它们。 在某些时候，政府可能会发现自己试图监管其技术同时依赖的人工智能提供商。

这不是公司与监管机构之间的正常关系。

当一家科技公司开始看起来像一个机构时

我们之前已经看到过这样的迹象。 政府已经严重依赖私人控制的云基础设施。 苹果可以决定哪些软件可以覆盖超过 10 亿台设备。 Cloudflare 可以确定互联网的某些部分在受到攻击时是否仍可访问。 谷歌对人们查找的信息有着巨大的影响力。 微软和亚马逊运营着世界各地政府、军队和关键行业使用的基础设施。 这些公司都不是宪法意义上的主权公司，但它们都控制着现代国家无法轻易复制的东西。

人工智能可以进一步增强这种依赖性，因为人工智能不是用于单一狭隘目的的基础设施。 它越来越多地被开发为认知工作本身的基础设施。

如果一个系统可以编写软件、识别网络漏洞、分析情报、设计分子、解释立法、生成政治信息和运行业务流程，那么对该系统的控制就是一种特别不寻常的权力形式。 运营它的公司也许能够通过改变价格、准入规则、安全政策或技术能力来影响整个经济活动类别。 目前看起来像产品管理的决策可能会开始类似于公共政策。

这就是鲍尔的想法变得有趣的原因。 事实上，对于能够制衡政府的机构存在着令人尊敬的论点。 民主社会故意充满这样的人。 法院限制民选政客。 独立媒体揭露政府不当行为。 大学挑战政治正统。 公司可以拒绝非法要求。 民间社会组织的存在正是因为集中的国家权力是危险的。

因此，仅仅因为政府是政府就认为政府应该自动控制最有能力的人工智能系统是错误的。 各国都有自己的监视、审查、政治胁迫和技术滥用记录。 一个对极其强大的人工智能拥有独家控制权的政府可能比拥有多个独立参与者的人工智能行业更可怕。

鲍尔的立场也比简单地要求放松管制更加微妙。 他认为，未来的某些人工智能功能可能非常危险，以至于“实际上不能将它们留在私人手中”。 能够实现生物武器、高度先进的网络行动或其他形式的灾难性伤害的系统最终可能需要更强有力的国家参与。 换句话说，争论并不一定是私营公司应该取代政府。 私人权力和国家权力之间的界限可能需要重新划定。

但一旦人工智能公司开始将自己视为能够制衡政府的机构，一个明显的问题就会出现：政府也有制衡力量。 谁为人工智能公司提供制衡力量？

没有选举的权力

这个问题比听起来更难，因为公司从来就不是为了具有这种制度合法性而设计的。 尽管政府有种种失败，但它们都是围绕旨在限制权力的机制建立的。 民选官员可以被罢免。 政府的决定可以在法庭上受到质疑。 公共机构根据行政法、宪法限制、披露要求和政治审查运作。 这些保护并不完善，而且各国之间差异很大，但原则很明确：一个机构拥有的强制权力越多，社会就越期望有机制对这种权力负责。

人工智能公司的首席执行官以一种截然不同的方式承担责任。 用户不投票给董事会。 示范政策未经议会通过。 内部安全决策通常不受信息自由法的约束。 公司可以重组其领导层，重写其服务条款，停止产品或改变对模型的访问，而无需任何类似于民主正当程序的东西。

对于普通软件来说，这主要是商业问题。 如果电子邮件应用程序更改其条款，客户可以投诉或离开。 但想象一下，人工智能系统已经嵌入医院、大学、政府部门和数千家公司。 想象一下，数百万工人依靠它来完成工作。 想象一下政府机构依赖它来进行网络安全或分析。

到那时，提供商开始看起来不再像软件供应商，而更像关键基础设施。

社会对待关键基础设施的方式有所不同，这是有原因的。 银行面临资本要求，因为它们的倒闭可能会损害周围的每个人。 公用事业公司有连续性义务，因为当供电变得不方便时，电力不能简单地消失。 电信公司的运营规则反映了其对社会的重要性。 一项服务变得越不可或缺，我们就越不愿意将有关它的每一个决定完全交给其所有者自行决定。

如果前沿人工智能真的像开发者所期望的那样重要，那么类似的问题最终也会出现在人工智能公司的门口。 经济关键模型的提供商是否应该有连续性要求？ 如果访问被终止，客户是否应该提出某种形式的上诉？ 政府是否应该能够在狭义的情况下要求互操作性或紧急访问？ 是否应该对关键基础设施内部使用的系统进行独立审核？ 如果模范提供者决定退出一个医院、企业和公共机构已经依赖的国家，会发生什么？

这些问题都没有一个简单的答案，而急于监管假设的问题可能会产生自己的问题。 但它们说明了为什么将人工智能公司描述为政府的制衡会产生后果。 机构权力很少伴随着机构义务。

如果人工智能取代工作，谁取代税基？

税收是这些义务之一，尽管可能不是最重要的一项。

如果人工智能系统使大量人类工作实现自动化，政府最终可能会面临实际的财政问题。 现代税收制度从就业中收取巨额收入。 工人缴纳所得税。 雇主缴纳工资税。 工资为消费提供资金，从而产生额外的税收收入。 如果其中一些工作从受薪员工转移到机器智能，经济产出可能会保持不变，甚至大幅增长，而政府征收收入的方式也会发生变化。

这并不能自动证明对人工智能征收惩罚性税是合理的。 对新兴技术征税只是为了降低自动化的吸引力，这将是保护效率低下的现有企业并推动其他地方创新的好方法。 但如果人工智能公司在预测系统能够取代大量认知劳动时是认真的，那么政策制定者就有理由询问税收制度最终是否应该跟随这一活动。

其中一项提议是所谓的“象征税”：对大规模商业人工智能推理征收极少量的税。 代币很有吸引力，因为人工智能提供商已经对它们进行计费，这意味着使用情况是可以观察到的，而模糊定义的“机器人”的工作则不然。 然而，代币也是一个不完善的税基。 不同的模型以不同的方式对语言进行标记，推理系统可能会使用大量内部标记，自托管模型使执行变得复杂，而明天的人工智能架构可能不会以类似于今天的形式使用标记。 计算、能源使用、企业利润或其他一些衡量标准可能被证明更为明智。

在这个阶段，精确的机制并不重要，讨论背后的原则才是重要的。 如果越来越多的经济活动从人力转向私人控制的机器智能，政府最终将不得不决定现有的公共服务资助系统是否仍然有意义。

税收只是更广泛问题的一个例子。 政府除了收钱之外还做一些事情。 它们提供连续性、安全性、争端解决、应急响应、基础设施，以及至少在民主国家中公众可以挑战机构权力行使的机制。 如果人工智能公司希望被视为比普通企业更重要的东西——能够平衡国家的机构——那么对话就不能停止于它们不受政府控制的自由。 它还必须包括变得不可或缺的责任。

OpenAI 已经陷入矛盾之中

这里有一个特别有趣的紧张关系，因为鲍尔的观点不应被误认为是 OpenAI 政策的官方声明。 OpenAI 本身倡导为前沿人工智能建立持久的联邦框架，并在安全、基础设施和国家安全方面与政府合作投入了大量精力。 该公司并未公开主张国家应该从人工智能治理中消失。

如果说有什么不同的话，那就是这些职位的共存告诉了我们有关该行业发展方向的一些重要信息。 人工智能公司可能希望政府参与某些领域，而在其他领域则抵制政府参与。 政府可能会试图监管人工智能公司，同时变得依赖它们的技术。 双方都可能拥有对方无法轻易忽视的影响力。

这种关系最终可能类似于强大机构之间的谈判，而不是传统的行业监管。

这种前景应该会让政治光谱双方的人都感到有些不安。

那些对政府权力持怀疑态度的人应该考虑他们愿意赋予没有民主授权的公司多少权力。 那些支持强有力监管的人应该考虑将先进的人工智能能力集中在国家内部是否会带来危险。 科技公司应该认识到，这种争论是双向的：如果他们希望社会接受前沿实验室应该独立，因为它们可以对政府进行检查，那么社会就有权询问应该对它们进行什么检查。

真正的问题不是谁赢了

也许整个讨论都为时过早。 人工智能的进展可能会放缓。 模型可能会商品化。 开源系统可能会阻止任何小规模公司积累现在所想象的那种力量。

但构建前沿人工智能的人们显然并不认为这是最有可能的未来。 他们在基础设施上花费了数千亿美元，招募政策制定者和国家安全官员，并公开讨论可以改变大部分经济的系统。

我们也许应该认真对待他们的雄心壮志，思考他们的后果。 人工智能实验室作为制衡政府的想法提出的最重要的问题不是是否应该允许 OpenAI、Anthropic 或谷歌变得强大。 如果他们的技术继续改进，他们可能会变得更加强大。

真正的问题是，当一家私营公司变得足够强大，以至于“它只是一家公司”不再能充分描述它的本质时，会发生什么。
